course: The Human Brain (MIT 9.13, Kanwisher) — reasoning about minds from evidence
goal: Given a behavior or deficit, predict whether it points to a dedicated brain module vs. distributed/domain-general processing, and say what evidence would tell them apart.
owned_prior: Systems/engineering intuition: you find out if a system has a dedicated component by disabling it and seeing what breaks vs. what doesn't.

cruxes.title: One ability, or two?
cruxes.hook: Bob loses navigation but nothing else — does that prove navigation is a separate piece of mind, or did the hardest task just break first?
cruxes.owns: engineering prior: under load, the weakest path degrades first; a single failure never tells you which component broke

cruxes.title: Correlation in the brain isn't causation
cruxes.hook: fMRI lights up for faces — that's a correlation. What would it take to show this tissue causes face recognition?
cruxes.owns: double dissociation from crux 1 — now we ask WHERE and WHETHER causally

cruxes.title: Does 'responds more' mean 'represents'?
cruxes.hook: Haxby's attack on the FFA: it prefers faces, but its activity pattern still discriminates chairs from cars. Debunked?
cruxes.owns: causal tools from crux 2 — now armed with intervention, ask what's actually represented

cruxes.title: When the framework should say 'no module here'
cruxes.hook: The 20-category scan found nothing for snakes, tools, flowers, food, cars — only faces/places/bodies/text replicate.
cruxes.owns: full toolkit from cruxes 1-3 — now used to falsify, not just confirm

cruxes.title: Coda: where do modules come from?
cruxes.hook: Bob never regained navigation as an adult. Children with equivalent damage often do.
cruxes.owns: closes the loop on crux 1's architecture question — is it built-in or built by experience
